Unlike standard INRs that may only fit data values, Geometric INRs explicitly regularize the differential properties of the implicit function to ensure the zero-level set represents a clean, regular surface without spurious components [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that standard approaches (fitting data values like f(pi)=0 and gradient=normal) can result in 'spurious components on the zero-level set' if not handled. It further explains that Geometric INRs address this by enforcing geometric properties, specifically the Eikonal equation (||∇f|| ≈ 1) and normal alignment, via regularization terms in the loss function. This regularization ensures the implicit function approximates a Signed Distance Function (SDF) of a 'regular surface', thereby avoiding the spurious components mentioned in the claim.

A Geometric Implicit Neural Representation (Geometric INR) is a neural network $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that approximates a Signed Distance Function (SDF) of a regular surface $S$, characterized by the property that the magnitude of its gradient is approximately unity ($\|\nabla f\| \approx 1$) [S1].

The claim states that a Geometric Implicit Neural Representation (Geometric INR) is a neural network $f: R^3 -> R$ approximating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) of a regular surface S, characterized by the property that the magnitude of its gradient is approximately unity ($||∇f|| ≈ 1$). Source [S1] explicitly defines a geometric INR as 'a neural network f : R3 → R approximating a SDF of a regular surface S, i.e. ||∇f|| ≈ 1'. It further explains that this property relates to the Eikonal equation ($||∇f|| = 1$) and is enforced via regularization terms in the loss function. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
